Lesson 9: Statics I - Balancing Forces and Torques
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:32:56 t V

That is, you'll still be solving problems, but we'll focus on physical situations where nothing is happening. There might be some pulleys or rods or balls, but they have no acceleration and all the forces balance.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:33:25 t V
The study of situations like that is statics, and there are usually a couple of statics questions on the F=ma.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:33:35 t V
We'll look at problems from two different perspectives today:

1) Forces and Torques

2) Energy
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:33:45 t V
Both methods are important, but some problems are easier with (1) and others are easier with (2).
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:33:50 t V

One way to describe this is that the ball feels zero force there (because the slope of the walls is zero). This leads us to the principle:
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:35:41 t V
Objects in equilibrium have no net force on them.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:35:49 t V
In math:
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:35:51 t V
→FNet=∑i→Fi=0F→Net=∑iF→i=0
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:36:04 t V
Is my notation clear?
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:36:30 t V
We will later extend this to say that there's also no rotational acceleration, so
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:36:36 t V
Objects in equilibrium have no net torque on them.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:36:38 t V
→τNet=∑i→τi=0τ→Net=∑iτ→i=0
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:36:44 t V
Same idea.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:36:58 t V
However, there's another description that is just as good. The ball is at the bottom of the valley, where its energy is lowest. Another way to describe equilibrium is
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:37:06 t V
When there are no external forces on an object, it can be in equilibrium at its lowest possible potential energy state.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:37:18 t V
FNet=−ΔUΔx=0FNet=−ΔUΔx=0 where UU is the potential energy.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:37:32 t V
Those of you further down the calculus pipeline this can be written as a vector result: →FNet=−∇UF→Net=−∇U

Objects with no outside forces can also be in equilibrium at their highest possible potential energy states.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 19:42:44 t V
These high-energy equilibrium states are less common in the real world because if we gave the ball a little push, it would run away down the hill. It has to be perfectly balanced to stay at the top. So it's called an "unstable" equilibrium. But both these types can sometimes show up in problems.

Additionally, we know that the rope will slide down the wedge (i.e. it will continue to move farther from the equilibrium point) if we slightly tug on one end of it. This is the behavior of an unstable equilibrium, which happens at a potential energy maximum.

We know from our earlier result the ropes are in unstable equilibrium when the ends are even. We are getting closer to even with our little snip.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 20:07:13 t V
Let me rephrase slightly:
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 20:07:16 t V
Another way to think about this is that in the picture the rope will start sliding to the left if we let it go (compare to the equilibrium configuration). Since our unstable equilibrium represents a potential maximum this configuration must be somewhat below that maximum. By moving a small piece from left to right we bring the entire rope closer to its unstable equilibrium position thereby raising the potential energy.

Here is our next principle:
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 20:51:47 t V
When a system has an external force on it, it is in equilibrium when a small displacement increases the potential energy by the work done by the external force.

Summary
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 21:02:49 t V
In statics problems, we set the sum of forces on an object to zero and the sum of torques to zero.
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 21:03:04 t V
Alternatively, we can ignore forces and torques and imagine making a small displacement of the system. If it's in equilibrium, the change in the system's potential energy is zero (if there are no external forces) or equal to the work done by external forces (if they exist).
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 21:03:23 t V
(Watch for a couple examples on the message board)
jonjoseph 2025-08-06 21:03:27 t V
When calculating torques, it is often useful to choose the axis about which we calculate torque strategically. This can simplify the torque calculation, especially if we choose the axis so that an unknown force has zero moment arm.
